hints: A vector equation of a line needs one point on the line and a direction vector parallel to it.
Subtract the position vector of $A$ from that of $B$ to obtain a direction proportional to $(-1,-3,1)$.
Use either $A$ or $B$ as the fixed point and attach a new scalar parameter to the direction vector, with $\mathbf r$ on the left.
walkthrough:
Write down the position vectors of points $A$ and $B$ in column vector notation:
$$\vec{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$$

Calculate the direction vector $\vec{AB}$ from $A$ to $B$ by subtracting the position vectors:
$$\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - 2 \\ -2 - 1 \\ 2 - 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = -\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$

Form the vector equation of the straight line through $A$ and $B$ using the position vector $\vec{OA}$ and a scalar parameter $\lambda$:
$$\mathbf{r} = \vec{OA} + \lambda\vec{AB}$$
$$\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}) + \lambda(-\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$$
*(or equivalently using point $B$: $\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}) + \lambda(-\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$)*

ai_rubric.Finding Equations of Straight Lines: Derives direction vector $-\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+\mathbf k$. Derives $\mathbf r=2\mathbf i+\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\lambda(-\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+\mathbf k)$, or $\mathbf r=\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k+\lambda(-\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+\mathbf k)$.

hints: Use the scalar-product formula for the angle between the direction vectors of $AB$ and $l$.
Take direction vectors $(-1,-3,1)$ and $(1,-3,-2)$, then calculate their dot product and both magnitudes.
Evaluate $\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}\right)$ in degrees and select the acute angle.
walkthrough:
Identify the direction vectors of line $AB$ and line $l$:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$$

Compute the scalar product $\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2$ step by step:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2 = (-1)(1) + (-3)(-3) + (1)(-2)$$
$$= -1 + 9 - 2 = 6$$

Calculate the magnitude of each direction vector:
$$|\mathbf{d}_1| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-3)^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{1 + 9 + 1} = \sqrt{11}$$
$$|\mathbf{d}_2| = \sqrt{1^2 + (-3)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{14}$$

Use the scalar product angle formula $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2|}{|\mathbf{d}_1||\mathbf{d}_2|}$ for the acute angle $\theta$:
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{11}\sqrt{14}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{154}}$$

Evaluate the numerical value and find $\theta$ in degrees:
$$\sqrt{154} \approx 12.4096737$$
$$\cos\theta = \dfrac{6}{12.4096737} \approx 0.4834938$$
$$\theta = \arccos(0.4834938) \approx 61.0863^\circ$$

Round the angle correct to 1 decimal place:
$$\theta = 61.1^\circ$$

ai_rubric.Using Scalar Products: Calculates by the process for evaluating the scalar product of the direction vectors, $(-1,-3,1)\cdot(1,-3,-2)=-1+9-2$. Applies the process for the moduli, Divides by the displayed product and take the inverse cosine. Derives $61.1^\circ$. The final result is $61.1^\circ$.

hints: Two vector lines intersect only if one pair of parameter values makes all three coordinate components equal.
Write general points as $(2-\lambda,1-3\lambda,1+\lambda)$ on $AB$ and $(1+\mu,2-3\mu,-3-2\mu)$ on $l$.
Equate two pairs of components and solve for $\lambda$ and $\mu$.
Substitute those parameter values into the remaining component equation; its failure establishes that the lines do not intersect.
walkthrough:
Express a general position vector on line $AB$ in terms of parameter $\lambda$:
$$\mathbf{r}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - \lambda \\ 1 - 3\lambda \\ 1 + \lambda \end{pmatrix}$$

Express a general position vector on line $l$ in terms of parameter $\mu$:
$$\mathbf{r}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + \mu \\ 2 - 3\mu \\ -3 - 2\mu \end{pmatrix}$$

Equate the two position vectors component by component to obtain three linear equations in $\lambda$ and $\mu$:
$$x\text{-component: } 2 - \lambda = 1 + \mu \quad [\text{Equation 1}]$$
$$y\text{-component: } 1 - 3\lambda = 2 - 3\mu \quad [\text{Equation 2}]$$
$$z\text{-component: } 1 + \lambda = -3 - 2\mu \quad [\text{Equation 3}]$$

Rearrange [Equation 1] to express $\lambda$ in terms of $\mu$:
$$\lambda = 2 - 1 - \mu = 1 - \mu$$

Substitute $\mu = \dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{3}$ into [Equation 3] to check for consistency:
$$\text{Left side of [Equation 3]} = 1 + \lambda = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$$
$$\text{Right side of [Equation 3]} = -3 - 2\mu = -3 - 2\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -3 - \dfrac{4}{3} = -\dfrac{13}{3}$$

Conclude that since $\dfrac{4}{3} \neq -\dfrac{13}{3}$, the three component equations cannot be satisfied simultaneously by any pair of values for $\lambda$ and $\mu$.
Therefore, the line through $A$ and $B$ does not intersect the line $l$.

ai_rubric.Vector Line Intersections: Expresses a general point of $AB$ or $l$ in component form, for example $(2-\lambda,1-3\lambda,1+\lambda)$ or $(1+\mu,2-3\mu,-3-2\mu)$. Equates at least two pairs of components and solves for $\lambda$ or $\mu$. The component equations are inconsistent, so the lines do not intersect.
